meta.subtitle: A Feasibility Study of a Balloon-Assisted Reusable Hypergolic Sounding Rocket for Low-Cost Near-Space Access
meta.affiliation: CHIREC International School, Hyderabad, Telangana, India
meta.abstract: Project AKS was a student-led aerospace proposal, co-authored by the present authors, to design and fly a reusable hypergolic sounding rocket on a total budget below USD 25,000 (≈ INR 2,00,000). The mission concept aimed to make the vehicle the highest-flying student-led rocket in the world, attaining an apogee of roughly 70–100 km depending on the convention of measurement adopted, by releasing the rocket from an altitude of approximately 30 km beneath a hydrogen-filled high-altitude balloon rather than from a ground launch pad. The underlying motivation was to initiate a school-based, student-led sequence of innovations directed at reducing the cost of space research and space travel, with an explicit emphasis on sustainability realised through the reuse and recovery of vehicle materials. The high cost of space research, which is typically inaccessible to ordinary citizens, was identified as producing a global deficit in rocketry exposure for school students. This document records the propellant selection (unsymmetrical dimethylhydrazine, UDMH, with dinitrogen tetroxide, N₂O₄), the hazard assessment and proposed mitigation, the balloon-assisted launch architecture, component-level material selection, feed-system and engine-cycle studies, injector and nozzle selection, five candidate cooling strategies, the propellant-mass and lift-gas calculations, the balloon platform trade study, the regulatory permits identified as necessary, and the full bill of materials. The project was initiated in Stage 8 at the age of 13 (2022) and closed during IGCSE (Stage 9/10) owing to academic priorities. It was presented to the school principal and commended, but never left paper, on account of permit requirements, an absence of expert supervision, and the potential carcinogenic properties of the selected fuel.
meta.editionNote: This document is a typeset transcription, in preprint format, of the original Project AKS proposal written in 2022–2023. The technical content, argument, terminology, and numerical results of the original proposal have been preserved in full and without omission; the editorial work has been confined to organisation, sectioning, typesetting of equations and tables, and the addition of figure captions. Where the original proposal contained internal inconsistencies, arithmetic slips, or unit errors, these have been reproduced faithfully in the body of the paper and are catalogued separately in Appendix A, so that the original record and the subsequent review remain clearly distinguishable. Sources for all figures are listed in Section 16.8.

provenance.title: Provenance, Scope, and Status of the Project
paragraphs: Project AKS was a proposal, co-authored by the present authors, to build a hypergolic student-led rocket with a budget of only <25,000 USD, or approximately 2,00,000 INR. The team aimed to build the highest student-led rocket in the world, reaching up to 70–100 km in height, depending upon the conventions of measurement adopted, since the rocket launch would occur at a height of approximately 30 km with support from a weather balloon.

The key purpose was to initiate a school student-led series of innovations, and progress toward reducing the cost of space research and space travel, with a special focus on sustainability, which in the team’s conception was to be achieved through the reusability of materials. The high cost of space research, often inaccessible to locals or to ordinary citizens, created a lack of space and rocketry exposure for students, which the team felt was a global challenge.

The project was initialised in Stage 8 at the age of 13 (2022) and was closed during IGCSE (Stage 9/10) owing to academic priorities. The team had planned to use hypergolic propellants so that the range of conditions permitting high-efficiency combustion would be wider. Research was carried out on various forms of cooling in order to find something cheap but practical. The proposal was sent to the school principal, presented, and commended. The project nevertheless never left paper, on account of permit requirements, a lack of expert guidance, the potential carcinogenic properties of the fuel that had been selected, and related factors.

motivation.title: Introduction and Motivation
paragraphs: Rockets are magnificent inventions that functioned as the rocket fuel which propelled physics and mathematics to a level far beyond the moon. It was rockets that ignited every schoolboy’s dream of going to space and staring at the earth below him. It was rockets, and the idea of space travel, that made our minds consider the possibility of extra-terrestrial organisms. And most of all it was rockets that made us dream of having colonies in other worlds — the dream of expanding and exploring where no man has ever been before. And now it is our dream to prove to the world that CHIREC and its students can go to space; even though not physically, we can create a rocket that can, harnessing the wonders of physics, robotics, and the power of chemical reactions.

We strongly believe that we have the potential to achieve this herculean feat. We even have a great sustainability advantage, as we can accomplish most tasks in our very own campus and chemistry laboratory if we have the trained personnel. In addition, our rocket is completely reusable, and all of its components can be tracked, collected, refilled, and reused. Project AKS is our chance at proving to the world, and to India, that future scientists are more than capable of bringing Indian agencies such as ISRO to insurmountable amounts of glory, like those of NASA, SpaceX, and Roscosmos.

propellant.title: Propellant Selection

chosen.title: The chosen propellant combination
paragraphs: We have already identified an optimal propellant, characterised by its high density, low freezing point, and a remarkable specific impulse of 316.7 seconds. This propellant, unsymmetrical dimethylhydrazine (UDMH), is expertly paired with a non-oxygen oxidizer, dinitrogen tetroxide (N₂O₄), in a balanced 3:2 oxidizer-to-fuel ratio.¹ Our fuel is 100% hypergolic.

Hypergolic fuels are an amazing combination, in which we do not need to rely on failing or potentially unreliable ignition systems and possibly malfunctioning electrical engineering. The approach leverages the inherent chemistry of instantaneous reactions, ensuring mission success irrespective of potential machinery issues. In addition, the hypergolic state allows high density compared with liquid propellants, and does not require near-absolute-zero tanks like those of cryogenic propellants. With our formula and helpful testing from the chemistry division, our idea has a very likely chance of success. With this formulation and promising results from static fire tests, our project demonstrates a highly favourable prospect for success.

hazards.title: Hazards
paragraphs: There is only one hazard of this fuel: dimethylhydrazine is slightly carcinogenic pre-combustion, and highly flammable.

mitigation.title: Hazard mitigation
paragraphs: Dimethylhydrazine demonstrates a slight carcinogenic risk prior to ignition. However, we have devised a practical solution to address this concern. Our approach involves providing our tank specifications to the suppliers, ensuring that the tank can accommodate the precise quantity of unsymmetrical dimethylhydrazine required. This same tank will serve as the core component for our mini rocket. This streamlined process enables the supplier to fill our tank directly, eliminating the need for intermediate transfers and minimising our exposure to the chemical.

Moreover, even in the rare scenario of exposure, the associated risk is minimal, lasting for just 2 to 3 minutes. This is due to the fact that unsymmetrical dimethylhydrazine remains in liquid form at room temperature and releases fumes at a notably slow rate owing to its low vapour density. Additionally, once the fuel is safely stored in our tanks, there is no need for further manual intervention, as all functions can be automated through valve connections.

Furthermore, our pipes will be fabricated using highly corrosion-resistant SS321 (which has added titanium) and bolstered with multiple fill and drain valves. This approach effectively invalidates any potential shortcomings, rendering the project entirely foolproof.

ascent.title: Balloon-assisted ascent
paragraphs: On the design aspects of this endeavour, we have come up with an ingenious idea that can revolutionise space travel. Being completely original in large-scale high-mass rockets, using high-altitude research balloons can significantly reduce the cost of our project by nearly 25–30%. It involves strapping our rocket to a high-altitude hydrogen balloon, which will balance our rocket until it reaches the point of a whopping 30 km high. In order to achieve this altitude, we have pushed the buoyancy and gas laws to the absolute limit and found our perfect gas: hydrogen.

In specific, 250 kg of hydrogen and a 300 kg rocket. Hydrogen is the lightest and one of the most abundant elements in nature. Complemented by its low price and harmless environmental impact, it increases efficiency while being nearly 40% more environmentally friendly than other giant space projects, making the first step into environmentally friendly rockets.

release.title: Release, ignition, and the propulsion train
paragraphs: At an altitude of 30 km the balloon pops, since the atmospheric pressure is too low. So, at an altitude of around 29 km, which will be detected using a barometric altimeter, the showerhead fuel injectors will be programmed to spray the oxidizer and fuel into the combustion chamber, which is made of graphite instead of SS 301 owing to the high temperature created by the reaction. The combustion chamber is connected to the exhaust nozzle, also made of graphite for the same reason, whose nozzle ratio will be 36.4 if a bell nozzle is used.³

footnotes.text: Section 8 states the intention to use an aerospike nozzle, and the bill of materials in Section 14 lists an aerospike with an expansion ratio given as 35:5. All three figures are reproduced as they appeared in the original proposal; see Appendix A.

airframe.title: Airframe, thermal protection, and payload bay
paragraphs: When we come to the actual rocket part of our project, we will build a 301 stainless-steel alloy model of the rocket, coated with polyurethane, which crucially protects the outer shell and body from harsh heating while near the ozone layer as well as while crossing the Kármán line. We also created a plan to transfer the oxidizer to the fuel chamber via metal valves controlled by an application or program.

In order for our rocket to be recorded and filmed, we have also created a chamber at the top of our rocket, with a mass of 5–6 kg, to place equipment that the school would like to send to space, along with cameras fitted at three different angles to capture the majestic launch.

feedSystem.title: Propellant Feed System and Engine Cycle Studies
paragraphs: The original proposal presented a sequence of feed-system and engine-cycle schematics that informed the architecture. These are reproduced in Figures 3a–6. The team’s own feed-system concept (Figure 3a) is a helium-pressurised arrangement in which a 5000 psi helium vessel feeds a pressure regulator, which in turn pressurises the UDMH fuel tank and the N₂O₄ oxidizer tank, each held at 3000 psi, with low-pressure fuel-rich and oxidizer-rich turbopumps downstream. The numbered annotations in the figure denote the ordering of the feed and pressurisation steps.

materials.title: Materials
materials.intro: Material selection was carried out component by component, as follows.

items.heading: The exterior of the rocket: stainless steel 301.
items.text: AISI 301 stainless steel (UNS S30100) is the most susceptible to cold-deformation strengthening among conventional austenitic stainless steels. Its work-hardening rate is extremely high: with each increase in the amount of cold work, the tensile strength and yield strength increase significantly.

items.heading: The tanks: stainless steel 321.
items.text: AISI 321 stainless steel (SS321) is basically type 304 with the addition of titanium (Ti), which stabilises carbides against sensitisation, so as to prevent intergranular precipitation of chromium carbide when the steel is heated to a temperature within the sensitisation range, such as during welding.

items.heading: The nozzle: SS 316 or graphite.
items.text: Final material selection is to be determined through thermal dissipation and strength at high temperatures and erosion testing and research.

injector.title: Fuel Injector
injector.intro: We have chosen a showerhead fuel injector, because such injectors possess the following qualities, which we need for our hypergolic fuel.

qualities.title: Efficiency.
qualities.text: Showerhead injectors are known for promoting efficient mixing of propellants, which can lead to better overall combustion efficiency. A higher combustion efficiency can contribute to a higher specific impulse, all else being equal.

qualities.title: Performance.
qualities.text: A specific impulse of 316.7 seconds indicates that the engine is already designed for good performance. A showerhead injector can help maintain or enhance this performance.

qualities.title: Thrust control.
qualities.text: While showerhead injectors are often associated with larger engines, they can be designed for variable thrust and precise control, especially with adjustable injector designs.

qualities.title: Combustion stability.
qualities.text: A showerhead injector can contribute to combustion stability, which is crucial for maintaining a high specific impulse and achieving high-speed, high-altitude flights.

qualities.title: Thorough mixing.
qualities.text: The even distribution of propellants in a showerhead injector can lead to thorough mixing, reducing the risk of unburned propellants and increasing overall efficiency.

rationale.title: Rationale and Projected Impact
paragraphs: Our conclusions suggest that we can reduce the price of space travel, and crash the aerospace stock market, if our project is successful. It will make aerospace voyaging more affordable. This is because the average cost of sending 1 kg to space is $4,000–$10,000, and our model can reduce that price to $1,000–$2,500, owing to our balloon epiphany.⁴

All in all, our progress is extensive. In the future, if our rocket succeeds, we plan to use thrust-to-weight formulae and GPS research to predict the location of our rocket and parachute post-ejection. We are also working on new and better nozzle designs based on the Titan rockets as well as the new NASA Artemis.

Now, we all may be wondering a fundamental question. Why us? And why this project? The question of why has fascinated us for eras upon eras. And even though it is a tough question to ask, it may be one of the simplest to answer. Why did Edmund Hillary climb Mount Everest? Because he saw a mountain and climbed it. And why did he climb the mountain he had just seen? Because he could. Why did NASA launch Armstrong to the moon, and Roscosmos launch Yuri Gagarin into space? Many of us would be speechless. But the answer was simple. Because they can. Because they could prove that mankind has no limits. The sky is no limit when there is a vast and endless void above the atmosphere. Space — the final frontier. And those technological giants saw it and wanted to conquer it. Why? Because they can.

comparison.title: Research balloons compared with weather balloons
comparison.intro: Research balloons and weather balloons are both types of balloon used for various scientific and atmospheric research purposes, but they differ in terms of their design, capabilities, and primary objectives.

rows.research: These balloons are designed for specific scientific research missions, often carrying scientific instruments, experiments, or payloads to gather data about the atmosphere, cosmic phenomena, or other scientific objectives. They are used for a wide range of research applications, including astrophysics, atmospheric studies, and Earth observation.
rows.weather: Weather balloons, also known as radiosondes, are primarily used for meteorological purposes. They carry instruments that measure atmospheric variables such as temperature, humidity, and pressure. The data collected from weather balloons helps meteorologists create weather forecasts and study atmospheric conditions.

rows.research: Research balloons can be much larger and have a higher payload capacity compared with weather balloons. They are designed to carry sophisticated scientific instruments and experiments, which may include telescopes, particle detectors, or other specialised equipment.
rows.weather: Weather balloons are typically smaller and have a lower payload capacity. They carry lightweight meteorological instruments, making them suitable for routine weather observations.

rows.research: Research balloons are often capable of reaching higher altitudes than weather balloons. They can ascend to the stratosphere, or even to the edge of space, providing access to specific research environments. Flight durations can vary from hours to several days or weeks.
rows.weather: Weather balloons reach altitudes up to the stratosphere, usually reaching an average altitude of around 30 kilometres (18.6 miles). They have relatively short flight durations, typically lasting a few hours, after which they burst and return to Earth.

rows.research: Research balloons carry a wide range of specialised scientific instruments and experiments tailored to their research objectives. These instruments may include telescopes, spectrometers, and sensors for various types of measurement.
rows.weather: Weather balloons carry meteorological instruments, such as radiosondes, which measure temperature, humidity, pressure, and sometimes wind speed and direction. These instruments are designed for weather forecasting and atmospheric profiling.

rows.research: Research balloon missions are less frequent and often involve significant costs, owing to the specialised equipment and research objectives. They are typically conducted by research institutions, space agencies, or scientific organisations.
rows.weather: Weather balloon launches are conducted regularly worldwide, often multiple times a day, by meteorological agencies and institutions. They are relatively cost-effective and play a crucial role in weather forecasting and monitoring.

comparison.summary: In summary, research balloons are specialised for scientific research missions with a focus on diverse scientific objectives, while weather balloons are primarily used for routine meteorological observations and weather forecasting. Both types of balloon contribute to our understanding of the Earth’s atmosphere and the universe.

medium.title: Medium scientific balloons
medium.intro: Medium-sized scientific balloons are balloons designed for scientific research missions that require a moderate payload capacity and altitude. These balloons are larger and more capable than small weather balloons, but smaller than the massive high-altitude research balloons used for specialised experiments at very high altitudes.

properties.title: Payload capacity.
properties.text: Medium-sized scientific balloons typically have a payload capacity ranging from several hundred kilograms to a few metric tons. This allows them to carry a variety of scientific instruments and experiments.

properties.title: Altitude range.
properties.text: These balloons can reach altitudes ranging from tens of kilometres (the stratosphere) to over 40 kilometres, depending on their design and inflation gas. They provide access to the upper atmosphere and near-space regions, making them suitable for atmospheric studies, astrophysical observations, and Earth science research.

properties.title: Flight duration.
properties.text: The flight duration of medium-sized scientific balloons can vary. Some missions may last a few hours, while others can extend for several days or even weeks, depending on the research objectives and the balloon’s design.

properties.title: Instrumentation.
properties.text: Medium-sized scientific balloons carry a wide range of scientific instruments and experiments. Depending on the mission, these instruments can include telescopes for astronomy, spectrometers for atmospheric studies, particle detectors, cameras, and sensors for various measurements.

medium.applicationsIntro: Medium-sized scientific balloons are used for a variety of research applications, including but not limited to the following.

applications.title: Atmospheric studies.
applications.text: Observations of the Earth’s atmosphere, including ozone measurements, climate studies, and pollution monitoring.

applications.title: Astrophysical observations.
applications.text: Observations of celestial objects, including stars, planets, and cosmic phenomena, at high altitudes so as to minimise atmospheric interference.

applications.title: Earth science.
applications.text: Collection of remote sensing data for Earth science research, such as land and ocean observations.

applications.title: Planetary exploration.
applications.text: Testing of instruments and technologies for planetary exploration missions.

launchRecoveryCost.title: Launch and recovery.
launchRecoveryCost.text: Medium-sized scientific balloons are typically launched from ground-based facilities, including balloon launch sites or research centres. They are often equipped with systems for controlled termination and recovery of scientific payloads.

launchRecoveryCost.title: Cost.
launchRecoveryCost.text: The cost of medium-sized scientific balloon missions can vary depending on the complexity of the research objectives and the equipment involved. They are more cost-effective compared with space-based missions, making them an attractive option for scientific research.

medium.closing: Medium-sized scientific balloons play a valuable role in scientific research, providing a cost-effective platform for studying the Earth’s atmosphere, conducting astrophysical observations, and advancing our understanding of the universe. These balloons are often operated by research institutions, space agencies, and scientific organisations dedicated to various research disciplines.

volume.title: Volume capacity
paragraphs: The volume capacity of medium-sized scientific balloons can vary depending on their design and specific research mission. However, a typical range for the volume capacity of medium-sized scientific balloons is approximately 100,000 to 1,000,000 litres (100,000 L to 1,000,000 L). This range allows them to carry a moderate payload while reaching altitudes in the upper atmosphere and near-space regions.⁷

We must keep in mind that the actual volume capacity may vary based on the balloon’s size and shape, and on the specific objectives of the research mission. Research institutions and organisations planning balloon missions work with balloon manufacturers to select or design balloons with the appropriate volume capacity for their scientific instruments and experiments.

footnotes.text: Note that 1,000,000 L is 1000 m³, which is smaller than the 2870.04 m³ requirement derived in Section 11.4. See Appendix A.

permits.intro: The following regulatory permissions were identified as necessary before any flight attempt.

notes.title: Specific impulse.
notes.text: Sections 1 and 3 gave Iₛₚ = 316.7 s, while the calculations in Section 11 and Table 1 used 317.6 s. The digits appear transposed. The difference is immaterial to the conclusions (about 0.3%).

notes.title: Oxidizer mass.
notes.text: The headline list in Section 11 gave 60.91 kg of N₂O₄, whereas the derivation and Table 1 gave 60.51 kg. The value consistent with m₀ = 301.27 kg and \(m_{\text{UDMH}}\) = 90.76 kg is 60.51 kg.

notes.title: Nozzle expansion ratio.
notes.text: The design section gave 36.4 for a bell nozzle, Section 8 selected an aerospike instead, and the bill of materials specified an aerospike with an expansion ratio written 35:5. These three statements are not reconciled in the original proposal.

notes.title: Mixture ratio sense.
notes.text: The 3:2 ratio was described as oxidizer-to-fuel in Section 3, but applied as \(m_{\text{UDMH}}{:}m_{\mathrm{N_2O_4}} = 3{:}2\) (fuel-rich) in the calculation, and labelled “fuel to oxidizer” in Table 1. The cited Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre data in Section 11.3 quoted peak Iₛₚ at an oxidizer/fuel ratio of 1.5, which is the reciprocal of the ratio used in the mass calculation. As written, the vehicle carried 1.5 parts fuel to 1 part oxidizer, whereas the performance figure it was credited with corresponded to 1.5 parts oxidizer to 1 part fuel.

notes.title: Feed architecture.
notes.text: Section 3.2 stated that helium pressurisation removed the need for turbopumps, but the feed diagram (Figure 3a) showed low-pressure fuel-rich and oxidizer-rich turbopumps, and the bill of materials listed two high-pressure turbopumps, turbines, gas turbine shafts, two preburners, and a 3000-horsepower electric generator. The original proposal therefore described a pressure-fed system in prose and a pump-fed, staged-combustion-like system in its diagram and parts list.

notes.title: Propellant named in the comparison.
notes.text: The specific-impulse comparison in Section 3.2 attributed 316.7 s to monomethyl hydrazine (MMH), not to UDMH, which was the propellant actually selected. The same item compared an exhaust velocity in km/s for ammonium perchlorate with a specific impulse in seconds; converting 316.7 s × g₀ gives about 3.11 km/s, which is roughly 1.3 to 1.7 times the quoted 1.8–2.4 km/s rather than “nearly twice”.

notes.title: The mass-ratio substitution collapses.
notes.text: In the step preceding Equation (13), the denominator \(\bigl(150 + \tfrac{5}{2}m_{\mathrm{N_2O_4}}\bigr) - \tfrac{5}{2}m_{\mathrm{N_2O_4}}\) simplifies exactly to 150, so the argument of the logarithm is m₀/150, which still depends on \(m_{\mathrm{N_2O_4}}\). The original proposal instead replaced the ratio with the pure number \(1 + \tfrac{5}{2}\), which removed the unknown from the equation. Consequently Δv was no longer a function of the propellant load, and the equation could not determine \(m_{\mathrm{N_2O_4}}\).

notes.title: Arithmetic slip in the logarithm.
notes.text: Equation (13) evaluated \(\ln\bigl(1 + \tfrac{5}{2}\bigr)\) as ln(2.5) ≈ 0.91629. In fact 1 + 2.5 = 3.5, and ln(3.5) ≈ 1.2528. The value carried forward corresponded to ln(2.5).

notes.title: Inconsistency with the final mass budget.
notes.text: Table 1 gave m₀ = 301.27 kg and \(m_f\) = 150 kg, a mass ratio of 2.0085. The rocket equation then yields
notes.textAfter: not the 2854.72 m/s of Equation (14). The propellant load and the quoted Δv are therefore mutually inconsistent by about 24%.

notes.title: No trajectory model links altitude to Δv.
notes.text: The 71 km altitude gain was stated as the objective, but no step connected it to a velocity requirement. A drag-free, constant-gravity estimate for a purely vertical coast gives \(v = \sqrt{2gh} \approx 1180\ \mathrm{m/s}\) for h = 71 km, which is a lower bound; gravity losses during a finite burn raise the requirement, and the true figure depends on burn time, thrust profile, and drag in the 29–50 km band. The value 2854.72 m/s was not derived from the mission requirement, and the agreement between the propellant mass and the altitude target was therefore not established by the analysis.

notes.title: Later algebraic steps.
notes.text: The step \(m_{\mathrm{N_2O_4}} = (m_f - 150)/(5/2)\) treated \(m_f\) as though it were m₀; by the original proposal’s own definition \(m_f\) is the structural mass of 150 kg, which would make the numerator zero. The subsequent line introduced the coefficient \(2.5 \times \tfrac{5}{2} = 6.25\), where the preceding equation contained \(\tfrac{5}{2}\) alone. The value 60.51 kg followed arithmetically from the numbers as written, but the chain of manipulations was not a valid rearrangement of the rocket equation.

notes.title: Temperature at 30 km.
notes.text: Equation (45) applied the tropospheric lapse rate of 6.49 °C/km continuously through 30 km, giving \(T_{\text{30km}}\) = 93.45 K. The International Standard Atmosphere has an isothermal layer at 216.65 K between roughly 11 and 20 km and warms above it, giving about 226.5 K at 30 km. The value 93.45 K is below the boiling point of nitrogen at one atmosphere, so the atmosphere it described would be condensed.

notes.title: Air density at 30 km.
notes.text: Even accepting T = 93.45 K and P = 2654.98 Pa, Equation (50) evaluated to
notes.textAfter: not the 1.03 kg/m³ recorded; the stated result was larger than the original proposal’s own inputs imply by a factor of about ten. The ISA value at 30 km is about 0.018 kg/m³, so the figure used was roughly 57 times too large. For comparison, sea-level density is 1.225 kg/m³: the value adopted for 30 km was close to sea level.

notes.title: Dimensional inconsistency.
notes.text: Equation (34) divided a weight in newtons by a density in kg/m³, which yields units of m⁴/s² rather than m³. The buoyancy condition should be written either as \(V = m/\rho_{\text{air}}\) or as \(V = W/(\rho_{\text{air}} g)\), and, more completely, as \(V(\rho_{\text{air}} - \rho_{\text{gas}}) = m_{\text{total}}\) so that the weight of the lift gas itself is accounted for.

notes.title: Mixed reference states.
notes.text: The volume was computed at 30 km but the hydrogen mass was obtained by multiplying that volume by the sea-level hydrogen density of 0.0899 kg/m³. A zero-pressure balloon is fully inflated only at float altitude, where the hydrogen density is roughly 0.0013 kg/m³. The two errors act in opposite directions, which is why the final figure appears plausible.

notes.title: Corrected order of magnitude.
notes.text: Taking ISA conditions at 30 km (P ≈ 1197 Pa, T ≈ 226.5 K, \(\rho_{\text{air}}\) ≈ 0.0184 kg/m³, \(\rho_{\mathrm{H_2}}\) ≈ 0.0013 kg/m³), the net lift is about 0.0171 kg/m³, so floating 301.27 kg requires roughly
notes.textAfter: with a hydrogen inventory of order 23 kg rather than 258 kg. This excludes the mass of the envelope itself, which for a balloon of that volume is substantial and was not budgeted anywhere in the original proposal. The required volume is therefore about six times the 2870 m³ derived in the original proposal, and the hydrogen mass roughly an order of magnitude smaller.

notes.title: Internal conflict with the balloon survey.
notes.text: The volume capacity quoted for medium scientific balloons in Section 12, 100,000 to 1,000,000 litres, is 100 to 1000 m³ — less than the 2870 m³ the design required by its own calculation, and far less than the corrected estimate above. The figures were most likely intended as cubic metres; large scientific balloons are of order 10⁵ to 10⁶ m³.

Section 10 claimed a reduction of launch cost to $1,000–$2,500 per kilogram. On the project’s own figures — a total budget below $25,000 and a payload chamber of 5–6 kg — the implied cost is approximately $4,200–$5,000 per kilogram, which lies inside the $4,000–$10,000 band the original proposal cited as the status quo. The claimed saving was not demonstrated by the accompanying budget, and the comparison is in any case between a suborbital altitude of 100 km and orbital launch prices, which are not equivalent services: reaching 100 km vertically requires roughly an order of magnitude less energy per unit mass than reaching orbital velocity.

Section 3.3 recorded a single hazard. Independently of any design question, the hazard set associated with the materials named in Section 14 was considerably broader than one item: UDMH is classified as a probable human carcinogen rather than “slightly” carcinogenic; N₂O₄ is acutely toxic by inhalation and is a severe respiratory hazard at low concentrations, a property the original proposal did not mention at all; hydrogen in the quantities discussed presents a large-volume flammability and detonation hazard; and pressure vessels at 3000 psi store substantial mechanical energy independently of their contents. The original proposal’s conclusion that the mitigation strategy renders the project “entirely foolproof” (Section 3.4) was not supported by the analysis it presented. This observation is consistent with, and reinforces, the authors’ own recorded reason for closing the project.

summary.title: Summary
paragraphs: The original proposal’s strengths were its architectural instinct and its scope. The central idea — releasing a small rocket from a balloon at about 30 km so as to avoid the densest atmosphere and the cost of a ground launch complex — is a real technique, historically known as the “rockoon”, flown by Van Allen and the US Navy from 1952 onward, and the choice of a storable hypergolic pair to avoid an ignition system is a coherent engineering response to the reliability problem the authors identified. The propellant survey, materials selection, permit list, and cooling options are all recognisably the right categories of question to ask.

The quantitative core, by contrast, does not close. The two principal calculations each contain an error that changes the answer by a large factor, and neither result is checked against an independent estimate; the trajectory analysis that would connect the propellant load to the 100 km target is absent rather than mistaken. Recovering the design would mean, at minimum, computing the required Δv from a trajectory model including gravity and drag losses, recomputing the atmospheric state at 30 km from standard-atmosphere tables rather than a single lapse rate, and sizing the balloon from a buoyancy balance that includes the envelope and lift-gas masses. That these gaps are visible at all is a function of how completely the authors documented the reasoning: the work records its own intermediate steps closely enough to be audited, which is more than can be said of most conceptual studies.
